displayTitle: A failed shortcut to the four-color problem became a problem of its own
discipline: Discrete geometry, graph coloring and measure theory

scope.note: OpenAI claims that arbitrary five-colorings of the Euclidean plane are impossible in ZFC, raising the unrestricted lower bound from five to six. The exact chromatic number remains six or seven.

originalQuestion: How many colors are needed for all points of the Euclidean plane if any two points at distance exactly one must receive different colors? Nelson's remembered motivation was to place map-coloring problems inside a single infinite unit-distance graph. That proposed shortcut failed, but the distance-coloring question survived.
modernQuestion: Determine χ(R²), the least k admitting a function c:R²→{1,…,k} with c(x)≠c(y) whenever |x−y|=1, with arbitrary color classes. This is the chromatic number of the plane's unit-distance graph; edges may cross, so it is not a planar-graph coloring problem. Requiring Lebesgue-measurable classes creates a distinct variant.
questionDifference: The OpenAI manuscript addresses the original unrestricted coloring problem, but claims only to exclude five colors: 6≤χ(R²)≤7, not an exact answer. Its stated bridge is an equivalence, in ZFC and for each finite k, between proper arbitrary k-colorings and weak measurable k-colorings. A weak measurable coloring may contain exceptional monochromatic unit pairs, provided their measure is zero when integrating over base points and unit directions. This is weaker than a proper measurable coloring and should not be substituted for it. The second claimed theorem excludes weak measurable five-colorings. Falconer's 1981 five-color lower bound assumed proper measurable color classes; it did not already exclude arbitrary four-colorings, and neither that theorem nor later results for polygonal regions settle the unrestricted version addressed here.

firstFormulation.label: Autumn 1950 in recollections; October 1960 printed formulation

attribution: Soifer's reproduced correspondence supports Nelson as proposer and Isbell as the seven-color constructor. Hadwiger supplied related earlier work and a 1961 publication. The name compresses these roles. Gardner's October 1960 column is the earliest printed formulation located through this historical account, not a proved universal priority claim. Classification: multiple origins and an unexpected offspring of map coloring.

uncertainty: The 1950 account is retrospective. Nelson and Isbell differed in recalling Nelson's lower-bound proof; Hadwiger's independent proposal remains uncertain. Gardner's complete column and Hadwiger's original papers were not retrieved. The date and transmission account rely on a scholarly history reproducing letters. No independent assessment of the 2026 proof is supplied.

events.title: The seven-color pattern predates the named problem
events.description: Hadwiger publishes the hexagonal seven-color construction in a different, restricted covering problem involving congruent closed sets. It precedes Nelson's unrestricted question rather than being its original formulation.
events.relationNote: An earlier construction later supplies an upper bound for a broader question.
events.uncertainty: The 1945 full text was not retrieved; its role is described by de Grey and Soifer.

events.title: A failed map-coloring shortcut leaves a new question
events.description: Nelson recalls seeking one infinite graph that could encompass map-coloring questions. He instead finds the unit-distance problem; Isbell recalls supplying seven colors.
events.relationNote: This records a remembered motivation, not a contemporaneous published formulation.

events.title: An infinite coloring obstruction must have a finite witness
events.description: De Bruijn and Erdős prove that a graph is k-colorable for finite k if every finite subgraph is k-colorable. In the plane, failure of k colors therefore entails a finite unit-distance obstruction, even if none is explicitly displayed.
events.relationNote: A general compactness theorem changes how the infinite problem can be attacked; direct historical causation is not asserted.

events.title: Publication and a small finite obstruction
events.description: Gardner prints the question after hearing it from Leo Moser. Hadwiger publishes it in 1961; the Mosers' spindle gives a seven-vertex obstruction to three colors.
events.relationNote: The printed record follows the remembered formulation by a decade.
events.uncertainty: The earliest printed statement located is Gardner's column as identified by Soifer; the full column was not retrieved.

events.title: Measure theory advances a different version
events.description: Falconer proves at least five colors are needed when all color classes are measurable. Payne later constructs a unit-distance subgraph on all plane points that allows two arbitrary colors but needs at least five measurable colors, showing why regularity cannot simply be discarded.
events.relationNote: This branch adds assumptions; it is not an earlier proof of the unrestricted five-color lower bound.

events.title: A finite graph finally rules out four unrestricted colors
events.description: De Grey constructs a non-four-colorable unit-distance graph, raising the unrestricted lower bound from four to five. The corrected manuscript has a 1,581-vertex example and describes computer search and independent verification using SAT solvers.
events.relationNote: Concrete graph construction progresses independently of the measurable restriction.

events.title: Five colors are claimed impossible; six versus seven remains
events.description: OpenAI claims that unrestricted proper colorings correspond to weak measurable colorings in ZFC and that weak measurable five-colorings cannot exist. This would imply 6≤χ(R²)≤7. The weak condition allows exceptional monochromatic unit pairs of product measure zero.
events.relationNote: The claim links the unrestricted and measure-theoretic branches without identifying proper measurable and arbitrary colorings.
events.uncertainty: Reported proof, not independently validated; exact chromatic number remains unclaimed.
